Tool-Call Dependency Structure is Linearly Decodable in LLM Agent Residual Streams

Tianda Sun    Dimitar Kazakov Affiliation: University of York Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Heslington, York Affiliation: YO10 5DD Email: tianda.sun@york.ac.uk Email: dimitar.kazakov@york.ac.uk
Abstract

Tool-using LLM agents produce trajectories whose calls form a directed dependency graph: earlier tool outputs supply arguments to later calls. Whether this execution structure is represented inside the model is unknown; prior structural probes have targeted static code or chain-of-thought text, not an agent’s run-time call graph. A low-capacity edge probe on the residual stream of Qwen3-32B decodes the tool-call dependency graph well above both a Hewitt–Liang random-label control and a positional baseline. A counterfactual contrast between value corruption and structural perturbation indicates the signal tracks abstract topology rather than identifier values, and replicates under an independent, non-substring oracle. The non-positional component replicates on three further interactive multi-hop benchmarks and attenuates as call order alone becomes a sufficient proxy for dependency, vanishing in single-shot planning. Per-layer activation patching shifts the probe at a later, non-patched boundary, evidence that the representation propagates rather than passively reads out, though the realised tool call does not move. To our knowledge this is the first structural probe of an LLM agent’s runtime tool-call dependency graph. Our claims concern representation, not behavioural control, and span two model families and one primary domain.

1 Introduction

Mechanistic interpretability has yielded sharp characterisations of how large language models represent linguistic and propositional structure: structural probes recover syntactic dependency trees from contextual embeddings (Hewitt and Manning, 2019), board-state probes reveal compact world models in game-trained networks (Li et al., 2023; Yuan and Søgaard, 2025), and dissection methods locate factual knowledge in middle-layer feed-forward modules (Geva et al., 2023; Heinzerling and Inui, 2024). These results share a methodological core: train a small probe to read an abstract structure from frozen activations, and use control tasks (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) and checks for interpretability illusions (Friedman et al., 2024) to verify that the probe recovers structure rather than memorising labels. Recent work has extended structural probing to numerical structure (Levy and Geva, 2025; El-Shangiti et al., 2025), propositional commitments (Feng et al., 2025), spatial world models (Li et al., 2026), and planning in chain-of-thought traces (Dong et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025).

However, the structural-probe literature has not engaged with a setting now central to deployed LLM systems: tool-using agents that interleave model generation with external function calls (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024). Agent trajectories carry a non-trivial structural object — the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tool-call dependencies, in which an edge i→ji\to j records that the output of call ii supplies an argument of call jj. Whether this dependency graph is encoded in the agent’s residual stream, whether that encoding is causal, and whether it is a property of agents in general or of one benchmark, are open, despite emerging interest in agent-state interpretability for behavioural drift (Wu et al., 2026a), retrieval auditing (Healy et al., 2026), and deception detection (Abdelnabi et al., 2024; Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

We address this gap with a Hewitt–Liang-style logistic-regression edge probe on the residual stream of Qwen3-32B (Qwen Team, 2025), conditioned on a positional baseline (Hewitt et al., 2021) so the signal is non-trivial (Figure 1). We make three contributions.

(1) The tool-call dependency graph is linearly decodable (§4.1): the inter-call dependency DAG of LLM-agent tool trajectories is linearly readable from frozen residual streams, above random-label, positional, random-init, surface-form, and probe-capacity controls.

(2) Topology sensitivity (§4.1): a counterfactual contrast indicates the probe tracks abstract dependency topology rather than identifier values; as supporting evidence that the representation is not a passive readout, per-layer activation patching shifts a later, non-patched probe readout, though the agent’s realised tool choice does not move.

(3) Cross-domain modulation (§4.2): the non-positional contribution follows a falsifiable prediction — positive on interactive multi-hop benchmarks (Ye et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025), vanishing where call order alone suffices (Shen et al., 2023) or transitive structure is absent (Patil et al., 2025) — and it reproduces on independently provided ground-truth DAGs (Shen et al., 2023).

§4.1 develops the first two contributions; §4.2 develops the third.

2 Related Work

Structural probes. The original Hewitt–Manning probe (Hewitt and Manning, 2019) read syntactic trees from BERT; subsequent work has read board states (Li et al., 2023; Yuan and Søgaard, 2025), propositional commitments (Feng et al., 2025; Heinzerling and Inui, 2024), numeric structure (Levy and Geva, 2025), and spatial coordinates (Li et al., 2026) from frozen activations. The methodological core is shared: a low-capacity probe reads off an abstract structure, validated with control tasks (Hewitt and Liang, 2019), conditional probing (Hewitt et al., 2021), and checks for interpretability illusions (Friedman et al., 2024). We extend this line by treating an agent’s tool-call DAG — and its transitive closure — as the probe target. The closest precedents probe graph structure — reasoning-DAG adjacency from hidden states (Zhong et al., 2026), static code data-flow edges (Troshin and Chirkova, 2022; Guo et al., 2021), and semantic-relation graphs decoded from text (Diego-Simón and others, 2026) — or scalar CoT plans (Dong et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; El-Shangiti et al., 2025); we differ in that our edges are side-effecting tool calls with an independently constructed ground-truth DAG (not tokens, static code, or text-derived semantic relations), and we add activation patching and a topology-vs-value dissociation these probe-only studies lack.

Agent interpretability. Recent work has examined retrieval-head identification (Wu et al., 2025), tool-output tracking (Abdelnabi et al., 2024; Healy et al., 2026), deception detection (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025), behavioural drift (Wu et al., 2026a), hallucination editing (Sun et al., 2025), and knowledge conflicts (Zhao et al., 2024). Closest to our setting, Tatsat and Shater (2026) probe agent residual streams for single-step tool-need and tool-risk (with feature ablation for a causal effect on tool selection), Sun et al. (2026) decode a per-step tool-necessity signal from hidden states, and Wu et al. (2026b); Wang et al. (2026) read and steer the chosen tool’s identity or intent from mid-layer activations. These decode per-step quantities (whether to call a tool, or which one); we instead decode the relational structure linking calls — the inter-call dependency edge (i,j)(i,j) — with per-layer activation patching of the dependency representation plus a topology-vs-value dissociation. The two approaches target complementary objectives: per-step decisions versus multi-step structure. To our knowledge this is the first structural probe of an LLM agent’s tool-call execution graph at the inter-call dependency level.

Tool-use benchmarks and the interactive×\timesmulti-hop axis. Agent tool-use benchmarks vary along two axes that turn out to matter for our analysis: whether tool calls are issued interactively with execution feedback or emitted in a single shot, and whether tasks require multi-hop chained dependencies or only direct ones (Yao et al., 2024; Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). The conjunction we rely on — benchmarks that are both interactive and multi-hop — is, by our own benchmark sweep, sparsely instantiated; we use this axis both to select evaluation benchmarks and as an explanatory variable for where our effect is measurable.

3 Method

We run Qwen3-32B (Qwen Team, 2025) as the policy of an agent in the retail split of τ\tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024), a multi-turn customer-service benchmark in which the agent answers user requests by issuing typed JSON tool calls against a simulated retail backend. Retail is our primary domain; §4.2.2 re-runs the identical pipeline, unchanged, on four further agent benchmarks to test cross-domain generality. We log the raw residual stream of all 65 representation layers (token embedding plus 64 transformer blocks) at every assistant decode boundary.

Oracle tool-call DAG.

For each trajectory containing ≥2\geq 2 tool calls we construct the oracle tool-call DAG (the binary edge label our probe will learn to predict): a directed edge i→ji\to j is added when a contiguous, case-sensitive, whitespace-normalised character substring of length ≥4\geq 4 of call ii’s output occurs verbatim in the serialised JSON arguments of call jj, i.e. call ii’s result supplies an argument of call jj — for example, if get_user returns a field user_id=123 and a later get_order call includes user_id=123 in its arguments, we add the edge get_user →\to get_order (exact normalisation and matching procedure in Appendix A; oracle code released). This length-≥4\geq 4 substring rule trades recall for precision; §4.2.2 shows the central finding also holds against an independently constructed ground-truth DAG (TaskBench), so it is not an artefact of the substring heuristic. Because the oracle uses textual overlap, §4.1.1 additionally pairs the residual probe with a non-residual surface-form decoder as a textual-overlap ceiling control. On τ\tau-bench retail this yields 1,1291{,}129 ordered pairs (i,j)(i,j) with i<ji<j across 105105 trajectories (286286 positive edges, 843843 negatives); the probe target is binary edge presence. We additionally define the transitive-only label set (§4.2.1): y=1y{=}1 iff ii is a multi-hop ancestor of jj in the oracle DAG and (i,j)(i,j) is not a direct edge.

Probe.

We train an L2L_{2}-regularised logistic-regression probe (C=0.01C{=}0.01, balanced class weights; StandardScaler fit on the training fold only; full hyper-parameters in Appendix A) on the concatenation xi​j=[H¯i;H¯j]x_{ij}=[\bar{H}_{i}\,;\,\bar{H}_{j}] of residual-stream vectors at the terminating boundary token of calls ii and jj, each mean-pooled across a fixed 7-layer set {0,14,28,41,50,57,64}\{0,14,28,41,50,57,64\} (final dimension 10,24010{,}240; the canonical V1 configuration of Appendix A). A linear probe of this capacity is a deliberately low-capacity reader (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Nordby et al., 2026): it can recover structure already linearly present in the residual stream but cannot synthesise it.

Evaluation.

We use per-trajectory leave-one-group-out cross-validation (logo; 105 folds on retail) so that no token from a held-out trajectory enters its own training fold; per-boundary CV leaks within-trajectory context and is excluded. We report AUROC over all out-of-fold predictions and a 95% BCa bootstrap CI from 2,0002{,}000 trajectory-level resamples. As the Hewitt–Liang random-label control (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) we re-run the full pipeline with edge labels uniformly permuted (500500 permutations for the main probe; 200200 for downstream variants) and report the empirical pp-value. To separate structural encoding from a within-trajectory positional prior — a probe could in principle predict edges from call ordering alone — we use conditional probing (Hewitt et al., 2021): a 5-feature positional baseline B=[i,j,j−i,nagent,j/nagent]B=[i,j,j{-}i,n_{\mathrm{agent}},j/n_{\mathrm{agent}}], with the residual probe’s AUROC gap over BB as the contribution we report (paired-bootstrap CI). For cross-benchmark evaluation (§4.2.2) resampling and logo are by task identity, effective NN being the distinct-task count. Probe weights, control distributions, and bootstrap raw data will be released.

4 Results and Discussion

§4.1 establishes the primary result — the tool-call dependency graph is linearly decodable from the Qwen3-32B residual stream under a full control battery (Table 1) — and adds supporting evidence from activation patching that the signal propagates rather than passively reads out. §4.2 shows the non-positional component generalises across three further interactive multi-hop benchmarks and attenuates where call order alone predicts the graph. We mark the evidential strength of each claim where it is made: decodability and its transitive extension are established under controls; the cross-domain attenuation is a descriptive tendency, not a fitted law; and propagation is representational, not behavioural.

4.1 Decoding the dependency graph

4.1.1 Pairwise dependency decoding

We first establish that the residual stream linearly encodes the pairwise tool-call dependency relation; §4.2.1 extends this to multi-hop composition. The controls below rule out the obvious alternatives — random-label learnability, positional templates, surface-form textual overlap, and probe-capacity effects (Table 1).

The probe recovers tool-call edges far above chance. The multi-layer V1 edge probe attains AUROC 0.869 over 1,1291{,}129 held-out pairs (95% bootstrap CI [0.801,0.930][0.801,0.930]; V0 reaches 0.870, Appendix A). No random-label permutation of 500 (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) exceeds it (p<10−4p<10^{-4}, Table 1), so the layer-pooled features carry edge information not recoverable from a model fit to random labels (Friedman et al., 2024).

The signal emerges in mid-stack layers. The per-layer profile (Figure 1, bottom; full control-band detail in Appendix C) is computed from seven individually-trained single-layer probes. The embedding layer (L0) attains AUROC 0.205; since an AUROC below 0.5 is a sign-inverted boundary, this is 0.795 once flipped, so L0 already carries edge information that the logo probe happens to fit with a flipped sign (a random-init L0 probe sits at chance, 0.533; Appendix C). AUROC then climbs sharply to 0.864 by layer 14 (∼\sim22% depth), reaches a maximum of 0.875 at layer 41, and remains in [0.855,0.867][0.855,0.867] through the final layer 64. This pattern matches reports of mid-stack semantic emergence (Belrose et al., 2023; Geva et al., 2023) and rules out a representation that is purely output-routing.

Decoded DAGs match the correct oracle more closely than structural shuffles. Against a structurally-scrambled oracle, the decoded DAG’s median edge-set symmetric difference (SD) shifts from 1.0 to 2.0 (Cohen’s d=0.84d{=}0.84, paired Wilcoxon p≈3×10−12p\approx 3{\times}10^{-12}); against a random other-task oracle, the shift is smaller (d=0.19d{=}0.19, p<10−4p<10^{-4}), reflecting τ\tau-bench retail’s shared task template. Both confirm trajectory-specific dependency structure.

The residual adds signal beyond position. A 5-feature positional baseline [i,j,j−i,nagent,j/nagent][i,j,j-i,n_{\mathrm{agent}},j/n_{\mathrm{agent}}] attains AUROC 0.792 under the same CV. Following Hewitt et al. (2021), a probe on [H¯i,H¯j;i,j,j−i,n,j/n][\bar{H}_{i},\bar{H}_{j};i,j,j-i,n,j/n] attains AUROC 0.869, a conditional contribution of +0.0775\mathbf{+0.0775} over the positional baseline (95% CI [+0.032,+0.127][+0.032,+0.127]; Table 1). A non-linear MLP on the same 5 positional features attains 0.7810.781, indistinguishable from the linear baseline. The same probe on random-init Qwen3-32B residuals contributes −0.053-0.053 (Heap et al., 2025), so the training-attributable gap, controlled for position, is +0.131\mathbf{+0.131} AUROC (non-overlapping paired CIs). This +0.0775+0.0775 pairwise contribution is the conservative baseline that §4.2.1 more than doubles on the transitive task.

The signal survives a stronger scaffold/template baseline. Augmenting the positional scalars with tool-name identity of calls ii and jj, their tool-name bigram, and call-distance yields a stronger template prior (AUROC 0.823 vs 0.792). The residual probe still contributes +0.0413\mathbf{+0.0413} over this scaffold baseline (95% CI [+0.019,+0.062][+0.019,+0.062], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0), and within matched tool-name-pair strata (23 strata) separates edges at within-stratum AUROC 0.774. The margin is smaller than the +0.0775+0.0775 over position — expected, as the scaffold prior is stronger — but positive and significant: decodability is not a scaffold-template artefact.

The residual probe beats a surface-form ceiling. A non-residual decoder on nn-gram overlap, tool-name features, and the 5 positional scalars (36-dim) attains AUROC 0.830; the residual probe exceeds this by paired Δ=+0.039\Delta{=}+0.039 (Table 1). Adding surface features on top of the residual probe gains only +0.001+0.001, suggesting the residual representation predictively subsumes the tested 36-dim surface feature set (Appendix C).

Input ablations. Across five feature variants (V0–V4), V0 and V1 attain AUROC ≥0.869\geq 0.869; restricting to a single endpoint or layer drops AUROC by 0.030.03–0.080.08, so we adopt V1 as canonical (Appendix A).

4.1.2 Topology-sensitive rather than value-specific

Does the probe encode the abstract dependency topology, or the specific identifier values flowing between calls? We compare its response to structural perturbations against matched single-field value corruptions.

Decoded DAGs match the projected oracle. Figure 6 shows four trajectories with ≥2\geq 2 tool calls; for each, we display the oracle DAG and the DAG decoded by thresholding the edge probe at its in-sample F1-optimal cut. On the agent’s pair space (oracle projected to the agent’s nn calls), per-panel SD is 0–2. The clean-condition whole-dataset distribution (N=105N{=}105) has median SD =1.0=1.0 (Appendix B). F1-thresholded decoded graphs are acyclic on all 208208 trajectories tested (105 clean ++ 103 corrupted), so no post-hoc cycle resolution is required.

Value corruption produces no detectable shift in the decoded structure. We apply a counterfactual at the median tool-call index of each trajectory: swap a single _id field in the call’s output with another valid id and rerun the policy. On N=103N{=}103 paired clean/corrupted trajectories the per-trajectory decoded-vs-oracle SD is statistically indistinguishable: median SD=1.0\mathrm{SD}{=}1.0 in both, mean shift Δ=+0.155\Delta{=}{+}0.155 edges, paired Wilcoxon p=0.11p{=}0.11, d=0.06d{=}0.06, drift AUROC 0.554 (Appendix B). Effective propagation N≈32N\approx 32: only 32 of the 120 corruptions land on a field a downstream oracle call would reference, so the non-rejection is underpowered against small effects; we interpret the d=0.06d{=}0.06 vs d=0.87d{=}0.87 contrast (paired CIs non-overlapping) as the load-bearing dissociation evidence, not the standalone null. The τ\tau-bench reward direction (clean 12.5%12.5\%, corrupted 18.3%18.3\%) is not statistically significant (Fisher exact p≈0.27p{\approx}0.27).

A structural positive control calibrates the value-invariance null. A structural perturbation that rewrites a single tool response to an empty result forces the agent to adapt its downstream plan (Appendix B). The decoded DAG on the intersected pair space differs from clean by median SD 1.0 (Wilcoxon p=1.18×10−11p=1.18\times 10^{-11}, d=0.87d=0.87, n=103n=103; 53% non-zero shift): the probe IS responsive to structural drift. Decoded-vs-oracle SD is unchanged in expectation (d=0.00d=0.00) because the task and its oracle DAG are unchanged by a response rewrite. The dissociation evidence is the contrast itself: a near-zero effect for value corruption (d=0.06d{=}0.06, approximate 95% CI [−0.13,+0.25][-0.13,+0.25]) against a large effect for structural perturbation (d=0.87d{=}0.87) on the same probe, the same pair space, and the same single-tool-call locality, though the two perturbations differ in magnitude. Whether a high-magnitude value perturbation would also leave the probe invariant is untested (Limitations).

The dissociation replicates on a second domain. This test must hold the downstream plan fixed — under free generation a value swap can itself trigger re-planning, which would move the decoded graph for a genuine structural reason — so we evaluate it under teacher-forcing. On ComplexFuncBench (185 paired golden-trajectory replays) the contrast holds: the decoded DAG is invariant to a same-type value swap (d=+0.018d{=}{+}0.018, 95% CI [−0.13,+0.15][-0.13,+0.15], including zero) yet strongly responsive to an emptied observation (d=+0.702d{=}{+}0.702, CI [+0.58,+0.83][+0.58,+0.83]; Wilcoxon p=1.5×10−16p{=}1.5{\times}10^{-16}). The topology-vs-value dissociation is thus cross-domain, not specific to τ\tau-bench retail.

An independent oracle reproduces the finding. A schema-typed value-equality oracle (no substring matching) agrees with the substring oracle at precision 1.01.0, as a strict subset that excludes exactly the substring-only edges most likely to be lexical. On this cleaner edge set decodability is itself high (direct AUROC 0.9470.947) and the conditional contribution over position rises to +0.289\mathbf{+0.289} (P⁡(Δ≤0)=0P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0); the per-layer activation patching also replicates (Appendix B).

4.1.3 Representational propagation

Decodability is correlational. Is the decoded structure load-bearing, or a passive readout? Per-layer activation patching offers supporting evidence for propagation: a source-call patch shifts the dependency readout, and the shift survives to a later, non-patched boundary (App E).

Across 80 minimal pairs differing in one oracle edge (Figure 8, App E), the feature-level patch is positive at every layer past the first fifth of the stack (peak Δpatch=+0.016\Delta_{\mathrm{patch}}{=}{+}0.016 at L57; L0 exactly zero), but is partly definitional since the patched layer feeds the probe. Read at a strictly later, non-patched call-jj boundary under a forward-propagating hook, the effect persists (Δdecodefwd=+0.0082\Delta^{\mathrm{fwd}}_{\mathrm{decode}}{=}{+}0.0082 at L57, CI [+0.0055,+0.0113][{+}0.0055,{+}0.0113]) and replicates cross-family on Llama-3.3-70B (App E). In neither family does the agent’s realised next call move (0%0\% shift). We therefore read this as evidence that dependency information propagates through the residual stream, not as behavioural control; behaviourally-sufficient and cross-domain causal interventions remain future work (Limitations).

4.2 Generality of the chain-composition signal

4.2.1 Chain composition

§4.1.1 shows the residual stream represents pairwise dependency edges. Whether it encodes the oracle DAG’s transitive closure — multi-hop provenance, i↝ji\leadsto j through intermediate calls — as a jointly coherent object is a stronger question (Figure 2). We test it at the same probe granularity, then check robustness to seed choice and model family, and characterise where in the stack the signal emerges.

The residual encodes multi-hop provenance better than direct edges. A transitive-only probe (label y=1y{=}1 iff ii is a multi-hop ancestor of jj and (i,j)(i,j) is not a direct edge; 103 positives across 105 trajectories) attains AUROC 0.986 (paired-bootstrap 95% CI [0.977,0.993][0.977,0.993]; Hewitt–Liang random-label margin +0.395+0.395, p<0.005p<0.005), versus the direct probe’s 0.869 on the same pool (Δdirect−trans=−0.117\Delta_{\text{direct}-\text{trans}}{=}-0.117, paired CI [−0.189,−0.055][-0.189,-0.055], P⁡(Δ≥0)=1/2000P(\Delta{\geq}0){=}1/2000). The model is more linearly decodable for “ii is a multi-hop ancestor of jj” than for “ii is a direct parent of jj” once a comparable negative set is used. Plausibly, transitive relations reflect more global trajectory-level plan structure; the gap may also depend on the negative pool, since the transitive-only label set excludes direct edges from the positives — the AUROC gap is therefore against a structurally easier negative set, not a stronger encoding alone.

The non-positional contribution more than doubles over §4.1.1. On the transitive task a 5-feature positional baseline attains AUROC 0.823; the residual-only V1 probe attains 0.986, a non-positional conditional contribution of +0.163 (paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+0.106,+0.222][+0.106,+0.222], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0/2000P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0/2000) — more than 2×2\times the +0.0775+0.0775 contribution on the direct task (§4.1.1). The joint minus residual-only difference is ≈0\approx 0: on this task position is fully subsumed by the residual representation.

Seed- and family-robust. Re-running the full pipeline on three Qwen3-32B seeds gives transitive conditional contributions +0.163+0.163, +0.155+0.155, +0.147+0.147 — mean +0.155 ±\pm 0.008 (each P⁡(Δ≤0)=0/2000P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0/2000; transitive AUROC 0.977±0.0120.977\pm 0.012, direct 0.889±0.0220.889\pm 0.022). This makes the result unlikely to be a lucky-seed artefact (SD 0.0080.008, 6×6\times under a pre-registered 0.050.05 threshold). Cross-family, Llama-3.3-70B replicates at +0.134+0.134 (paired CI [+0.093,+0.178][+0.093,+0.178], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0/2000P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0/2000; direct 0.912, transitive 0.967), only +0.021+0.021 from the Qwen3 mean, reducing the concern that the effect is Qwen3-32B-specific. We report +0.155 ±\pm 0.008 as the canonical chain-composition contribution; the single-seed +0.163+0.163 is its upper instance.

Composition co-emerges with direct dependency, not late-stack. Figure 3 re-runs both probes per layer. Both saturate at layer 14 (∼\sim22% depth); from L0 to L14 the transitive signal climbs +0.15+0.15 AUROC versus +0.07+0.07 for direct, and from L14 to layer 64 it stays a consistent ∼\sim+0.12+0.12 above direct. Chain-composition information is built up alongside direct dependency in the early third of the stack — the “composition is a late-stack operation” hypothesis is rejected here.

The signal strengthens with hop distance and is direction-sensitive. Stratifying the transitive pool (Appendix D): AUROC increases with hop count (1-hop 0.869, 2-hop 0.974, 3+-hop 0.995) and trajectory length (2–3 calls 0.942, 4–6 0.972, 7+ 0.998) — long-range reachability is decoded more cleanly than local edges. Applying the forward-trained probe to direction-reversed features drops AUROC from 0.869 to 0.724, so the encoding is direction-sensitive, not a symmetric co-occurrence detector.

Thresholded predictions are not transitively coherent. At each trajectory’s F1-optimal threshold, the binarised edge predictions show transitive consistency P⁡(i→k^∣i→j^,j→k^)P(\hat{i{\to}k}\mid\hat{i{\to}j},\hat{j{\to}k}) of 0.3070.307 versus a pairwise-independence null of 0.4290.429 (Wilcoxon p=0.999p{=}0.999 one-sided obs >> null) — below the pairwise-independence null. This is consistent with the representational claim, which does not commit to threshold-level decisional coherence: the residual represents the multi-hop graph (the +0.155+0.155 contribution above), while the thresholded decisions cluster on direct edges, which by construction do not form i→ki{\to}k triples through an intermediate jj. The representational signal has causal support at the probe-readout level (§4.1.3) and, as we show next, generalises across domains (§4.2.2).

4.2.2 Cross-domain generality

The cross-domain results match the qualitative prediction (three positive interactive multi-hop replications: τ\tau-bench retail +0.155+0.155, ToolHop +0.161+0.161, ComplexFuncBench +0.060+0.060; predicted-zero TaskBench −0.02-0.02; inapplicable BFCL; Spearman ρ=−0.80\rho{=}-0.80 / n=4n{=}4 a tendency, not a law).

If the chain-composition signal is genuinely non-positional, it makes a concrete, testable prediction: its magnitude must scale inversely with how well call order alone predicts dependency, and it must vanish where position already suffices (single-shot planning) or where no transitive structure exists (direct-only tool use). We test this prediction by re-running the §3 probe and evaluation pipeline — identical probe, logo grouping, and bootstrap protocol, with benchmark-appropriate trajectory collection (Appendix E) — on four further benchmarks spanning the interactive×\timesmulti-hop axis (Table 2).

The qualitative pattern holds benchmark by benchmark. Each interactive-multi-hop benchmark independently gives a strongly positive contribution with a tight paired-bootstrap CI and P⁡(Δ≤0)=0P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0 (Table 2), and the single-shot control vanishes (TaskBench −0.02-0.02, n.s.). These per-benchmark CIs — not a fitted trend — are the load-bearing evidence; the four effects are additionally rank-ordered by position-predictability (Spearman ρ=−0.80\rho{=}-0.80, n=4n{=}4), a descriptive tendency only (p≈0.33p{\approx}0.33), not a law (Figure 4). The airline expansion is excluded (effective N=13N{=}13, pre-registered ≥15\geq 15); τ2\tau^{2}-bench telecom is an underpowered corroboration only (Appendix E).

ComplexFuncBench shows the predicted attenuation. Its call order is markedly more position-predictable (baseline 0.8720.872), so the account predicts the contribution should attenuate yet stay positive — which +0.060+0.060 confirms; ToolHop (+0.161+0.161) instead matches retail.

The contribution vanishes at both predicted boundaries. The prediction also says where the contribution must disappear: single-shot planning, where generation order already encodes dependency, and direct-only tool use, where no transitive structure exists. Both boundary cases behave as predicted. On TaskBench (Shen et al., 2023) — single-shot, position-only baseline 0.8910.891 — the contribution is −0.02-0.02 (vanishes, as predicted); and because TaskBench’s dependency DAG is independently provided (not our substring oracle), its direct AUROC 0.8940.894 / transitive 0.8880.888 provides evidence that the decodability finding is not solely an artefact of the substring oracle. On BFCL multi-turn (Patil et al., 2025) — structurally direct-only (1 transitive-only edge in 4,5254{,}525 pairs) — the contribution is untestable by construction, while direct AUROC 0.960 over 197 distinct stateful tasks extends decodability to a further domain.

5 Conclusion

We trained a low-capacity edge probe on Qwen3-32B’s residual stream under Hewitt–Liang random-label and conditional-probing controls (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Hewitt et al., 2021). The tool-call dependency graph — pairwise and transitive — is linearly decodable from the residual stream; per-layer activation patching adds supporting evidence that this representation propagates rather than passively reads out (behaviour not moved). The non-positional component replicates on ToolHop and ComplexFuncBench and attenuates with each benchmark’s position-predictability, and a counterfactual contrast (two domains) indicates the signal tracks abstract dependency topology, not the identifier values flowing through it. More broadly, these results suggest tool-using agents expose a new class of mechanistic-interpretability targets: runtime execution structures, not only token-level decisions or reasoning traces.

Limitations

Scope of the propagation claim.

Our patching evidence is representational propagation, not behavioural control. Activation patching shifts the downstream dependency readout (feature-level, and propagation-robust at a strictly later, non-patched call-jj boundary; App E), yet the agent’s realised tool call does not move under the same intervention. This causal evidence is established on Qwen3-32B in the τ\tau-bench retail domain and replicates on Llama-3.3-70B, while decodability and the non-positional contribution are shown more broadly across benchmarks; cross-domain causal replication and behaviourally-sufficient interventions over many turns remain future work.

Models, scale, and agent setup.

We probe two open-weight models in the 32B–70B range; whether the same linear decodability holds at much smaller scales, or in closed frontier models, is untested. Trajectories are collected under a single agent policy and decoding configuration per benchmark, so sensitivity to the agent scaffold, prompt, and sampling settings remains uncharacterised.

Dependency-graph topology.

The benchmarks on which the non-positional contribution is established differ in dependency-graph shape; one corroborating benchmark (ToolHop) is composed largely of linear chains rather than branching DAGs. The contribution’s behaviour on richer branching topologies, and on agent domains with error-recovery or re-planning sub-graphs, remains to be characterised.

Oracle construction and positional baseline.

The retail oracle uses a normalised length-≥4\geq 4 substring match; an independent schema-typed value-equality oracle on the same domain (no substring matching) agrees with it at precision 1.01.0 and reproduces both decodability and the activation-patching result (Appendix B), and TaskBench’s independently provided ground-truth DAG (§4.2.2) corroborates cross-domain. Both oracles define an edge by a value produced at call ii reappearing in call jj’s arguments, so the construct is value-reuse dependency: a dependency mediated by a transformed value (e.g. a count or reformatted field) or by pure control flow (call jj issued because call ii returned, without reusing its value) lies outside both oracles, and “dependency structure” throughout should be read in this value-reuse sense. Agent-self-reported chains and full provenance instrumentation remain compatible with the same pipeline but untested. The non-positional contribution is measured relative to a 5-feature positional baseline; its magnitude depends on how strong that within-trajectory prior is in a given domain — we report this dependence as a finding (the domain-modulation of §4.2.2) rather than treating any single domain’s magnitude as the definitive effect size.

Appendix A Implementation Details

Model and inference. Qwen3-32B (Qwen Team, 2025) (HuggingFace revision prefix 9216db5) served in bf16 on one NVIDIA GH200 120 GB GPU per worker, with a decode-time hook capturing the residual stream at each transformer block for every assistant token. Trajectory generation: do_sample=True, temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95, top-kk 20, max_new_tokens=4096, max turns 32. Random seed 42 across Python, NumPy, PyTorch, and scikit-learn; identical seeds across clean and corrupted runs. The τ\tau-bench commit hash is recorded with the release artefacts.

Trajectory selection. We collect 120 retail task instances; after filtering trajectories with <2<2 tool calls, 105 remain. The pair space comprises 1,1291{,}129 ordered (i,j)(i,j) pairs with i<ji<j: 286 positives and 843 negatives.

Probe input. For each pair, the residual-stream vector at the token immediately following each tool call’s terminating boundary, mean-pooled across layers {0,14,28,41,50,57,64}\{0,14,28,41,50,57,64\}, then concatenated: xi​j=[H¯i(pool);H¯j(pool)]∈ℝ10,240x_{ij}=[\bar{H}^{(\mathrm{pool})}_{i}\,;\,\bar{H}^{(\mathrm{pool})}_{j}]\in\mathbb{R}^{10{,}240} (V1).

Probe training. sklearn LogisticRegression, L2L_{2} penalty, C=0.01C{=}0.01, solver lbfgs, max_iter=2000, class_weight=’balanced’; StandardScaler fit on the training fold only.

Cross-validation and CI. Per-trajectory LeaveOneGroupOut (105 folds on retail); AUROC computed once over concatenated out-of-fold predictions. Bias-corrected-and-accelerated bootstrap, 2,000 trajectory-level resamples. Hewitt–Liang control: 500 label permutations for the main probe (200 for downstream variants), probe refit from scratch each time; empirical pp is the fraction of permutations with AUROC ≥\geq observed.

Input ablations. V0–V4 vary which boundary tokens feed the probe and the number of pooled layers; V1 is canonical (Table 1).

Oracle construction (full specification). For an ordered call pair (i,j)(i,j), i<ji<j, let oio_{i} be call ii’s tool output rendered as text and aja_{j} the JSON serialisation (json.dumps, default settings) of call jj’s arguments. Both are normalised by s↦s\mapsto re.sub(r"\s+"," ",s).strip() (collapse every maximal whitespace run to one space; trim ends). We then enumerate every contiguous character substring of the normalised oio_{i} of length ≥4\geq 4, keep those that occur verbatim (case-sensitively) as a substring of the normalised aja_{j}, and discard any that is contained in a longer retained hit; an edge i→ji\!\to\!j exists iff at least one maximal hit remains. No lowercasing, stemming, tokenisation, punctuation removal, or Unicode normalisation beyond whitespace is applied. The transitive-only label set is the transitive closure of these direct edges minus the direct edges. For the causal test (Appendix E), the 80 minimal pairs are all trajectory pairs (A,B)(A,B) whose tool-name sequences share a common prefix and whose oracle DAGs differ in exactly one edge on that shared prefix; the differing edge defines the patched source call. Oracle-construction and minimal-pair-selection code are released with the probe artefacts.

Extended experiments. The transitive (§4.2.1) and cross-domain (§4.2.2) experiments reuse this pipeline unchanged. Multi-seed adds Qwen3-32B seeds 43 and 44; cross-family uses the unsloth/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct mirror (ungated, identical weights) with a matched fractional-depth layer set. Activation patching (Appendix E) is feature-level and all-cached (no additional model inference). Cross-benchmark runs group all logo folds and bootstrap resamples by task identity and report the distinct-task effective NN. Total compute is ≈\approx300–340 GPU-hours of an 2,800-hour budget (Python 3.10.20, kg_verl environment); the two cross-domain benchmarks together cost ≈\approx12–15 GPU-hours.

Appendix B Value-Corruption and Positive-Control Analysis

Counterfactual construction. For each of 120 source trajectories we identify the median-index tool call and swap a single _id field in its output with another valid id drawn uniformly from the same database table, holding all preceding state fixed. The corrupted trajectory is replayed from the swap point and the residual stream is recaptured.

Validation and effective propagation. The corrupted output remains schema-valid in all cases. The corruption is oracle-aware: we walk the corrupted call’s JSON for _id-suffixed keys, select the field whose value appears in the oracle’s downstream args, and flip 2–3 alphanumeric characters at that path. Of 120 source trajectories, 3232 (26.7%) register an oracle-target hit; on the rest the agent’s plan does not chain through the corrupted field or recovers via a fallback call. Effective NN for detecting propagation is therefore ≤32\leq 32; at this effective NN the paired Wilcoxon at α=0.05\alpha{=}0.05/80% power detects |d|≥0.50|d|\geq 0.50, so the observed d=0.06d{=}0.06 is uninformative about small effects while the contrast against the structural-control d=0.87d{=}0.87 is well outside the type-II zone.

Matched subset. Of 120 source trajectories, 103 (85.8%) have ≥2\geq 2 tool calls in both conditions; these form the N=103N{=}103 paired sample.

Reward audit. Clean trajectories pass τ\tau-bench’s binary reward at 12.5%12.5\% (15/120); corrupted at 18.3%18.3\% (22/120). The +5.8+5.8 pp difference is not significant (Fisher exact p≈0.27p\approx 0.27); we report it for transparency and do not treat the direction as evidence of anything.

Statistics. Paired Wilcoxon p=0.11p{=}0.11; Cohen’s d=0.06d{=}0.06 (approximate 95% CI [−0.13,+0.25][-0.13,+0.25] via Borenstein paired-dzd_{z} SE on N=103N{=}103); mean shift Δ=+0.155\Delta{=}{+}0.155 edges; per-trajectory drift AUROC 0.5540.554. Figure 5 overlays the clean and corrupted SD distributions; medians coincide at SD=1.0\mathrm{SD}{=}1.0.

Structural skip-tool positive control. For each of 105 clean trajectories with ≥2\geq 2 tool calls we identify the median agent call index m=nagent/2m=n_{\mathrm{agent}}/2 and replay with the tool response at mm rewritten to an empty result (literal "{}"); predictions were pre-registered (SHA-1 sealed before first inference). Per-condition decoded-vs-oracle SD: median 1.0 in both, Cohen’s d=0.00d=0.00, drift AUROC 0.545 — null in expectation, because the task and its oracle DAG are unchanged by a response rewrite. Plan-shift SD between clean and corrupted decoded DAGs on the intersected pair space: median 1.0, Wilcoxon p=1.18×10−11p=1.18\times 10^{-11}, Cohen’s d=0.87d=0.87, n=103n=103, 53% non-zero shift. Together these support the §4.1.2 interpretation: the probe is responsive to the structural perturbation but the adapted plan still solves the same task.

Independent (non-substring) oracle replication. To test whether decodability reflects abstract dependency rather than the substring rule itself, we re-derive the retail edges with a schema-typed value-equality oracle: an edge i→ji\!\to\!j exists only where a typed-ID value produced in call ii’s output (structured _id fields and bare entity returns such as find_user_id →\to "yusuf_rossi_9620") is passed under a typed-ID key to call jj, with no substring containment. This oracle agrees with the substring oracle at precision 1.0001.000 (every independent edge is also a substring edge), recall 0.7540.754, F1 0.8600.860, overall agreement 0.9100.910 over the 1,1291{,}129 pairs; it is a strict semantic subset (312312 vs 414414 edges) that excludes exactly the 102102 substring-only edges — the partial-overlap cases most likely to be lexical artefacts. Under these independent labels (per-trajectory logo, 2000-iteration bootstrap), the conditional contribution over the positional baseline rises to +0.289+0.289 (95% CI [+0.265,+0.315][+0.265,+0.315], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0); the positional baseline itself falls to 0.6580.658, as call order predicts genuine typed-field dataflow even less well than it predicts substring overlap. Re-keying the feature-level activation patching (§4.1.3) to the independent oracle reproduces the causal signature: signed Δpatch>0\Delta_{\mathrm{patch}}>0 with bootstrap CI excluding zero at four mid/late layers (L41 +0.001+0.001, L50 +0.020+0.020, L57 +0.245+0.245, L64 +0.006+0.006), embedding layer L0 exactly zero. Both decodability and the propagation result therefore survive a dependency oracle that makes no use of substring matching.

Appendix C Random-Init and Surface-Form Controls

This appendix details the conditional-probing analysis reported in §4.1.1 (Table 1, “Conditional probing” block).

Conditional-probing protocol. Following Hewitt et al. (2021): train one probe on a positional baseline alone, one on positional features concatenated with residual-stream features, and report the AUROC gap. The positional baseline is B=[i,j,j−i,nagent,j/nagent]B=[i,j,j{-}i,n_{\mathrm{agent}},j/n_{\mathrm{agent}}] (5-dim, no model); the residual features are R=[H¯i,H¯j]R=[\bar{H}_{i},\bar{H}_{j}] (10240-dim, V1). Same per-trajectory logo CV, a 200-permutation Hewitt–Liang control on the joint probe, and a 2000-iteration trajectory-level paired bootstrap on the contribution.

Positional baseline. The 5-feature probe attains AUROC 0.792 — a quantification of τ\tau-bench retail’s stereotyped find_user→\toget_order→\tomodify/cancel layout.

Conditional probe (trained Qwen3-32B). AUROC 0.869, joint CI [0.801,0.930][0.801,0.930]; 200-perm Hewitt–Liang CTRLmax=0.572{}_{\max}{=}0.572 (0/2000/200 exceed observed). The headline statistic is the paired-bootstrap contribution: +0.0775\mathbf{+0.0775} AUROC, paired 95% CI [+0.032,+0.127][+0.032,+0.127], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0/2000P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0/2000 (p<5×10−4p<5{\times}10^{-4}).

Conditional probe (random-init Qwen3-32B). Same architecture and tokenizer, random weights, forward-passed over the same 105 trajectories at the same boundary tokens (no resampling). AUROC 0.738; contribution −0.053-0.053 over the positional baseline, paired CI [−0.101,−0.007][-0.101,-0.007] (Heap et al., 2025). The two paired CIs do not overlap; the training-attributable, position-controlled gap is +0.131+0.131 AUROC.

Surface-form decoder. A non-residual decoder on nn-gram overlap between call outputs and downstream args, tool-name one-hots, and the 5 positional scalars (36-dim) attains AUROC 0.830 (paired-bootstrap CI [0.748,0.898][0.748,0.898]; predictions pre-registered before inference). Residual minus surface is +0.039\mathbf{+0.039} (paired CI [+0.012,+0.063][+0.012,+0.063], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0.0025P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0.0025); adding surface features on top of the residual probe gains only +0.001+0.001, so the residual representation predictively subsumes the tested surface feature set (representational subsumption vs. a regularisation ceiling is not separately established).

MLP probe. A 2-hidden-layer head (10,240→1024→256→110{,}240\to 1024\to 256\to 1, ReLU, dropout 0.2, Adam l​r=10−4lr{=}10^{-4}, early-stop) on V1 features attains AUROC 0.866 — no improvement over the linear probe (0.869), consistent with the structural signal being linearly readable.

Random-init diagnostics. Before adding the positional baseline the random-init multi-layer probe attained 0.755. (i) All-65-layer pool: 0.733. (ii) Position-only: 0.792 (above all random-init variants). (iii) L0-only random-init: 0.533 (at chance — the random-init signal is RoPE-propagated through depth, not embedding-localised). (iv) 200-perm Hewitt–Liang control on random-init: margin +0.159+0.159, p<0.005p<0.005.

Appendix E Cross-Benchmark Details

Activation patching. 80 minimal pairs of trajectories sharing a tool-name prefix but differing in one oracle edge; 1,750 patch observations. For each minimal pair (A,B)(A,B) and each differing pair (i,j)(i,j), layer LL of BB’s call-ii residual is replaced with AA’s layer-LL call-ii residual, the pooled probe feature is recomputed, and the signed shift toward AA’s oracle is measured. Estimator is feature-level mediation, all-cached.

Signed Δpatch>0\Delta_{\mathrm{patch}}>0 with bootstrap CI excluding zero at every layer ≥14\geq 14; the embedding layer is exactly zero (negative control). Peak absolute effect +0.016+0.016 at layer 57; direction consistent across the 80 pairs.

Forward-hook propagation evidence. The feature-level estimator recomputes the pooled probe feature from the patched residual; a linear probe’s output therefore moves nearly by construction when its own input is patched. We extend it with a KV-cache-safe forward-propagating hook: the patch is applied at layer LL on the prefill pass and propagates to all subsequent tokens, and the probe is read at a strictly later, non-patched call-jj boundary (same 80 minimal pairs).

At L57 the propagation-robust effect on the downstream non-patched boundary is positive with CI excluding zero (87.5% of 80 pairs); L0 (negative control) CI includes zero. L41 shows a significant negative deflection that we report rather than hide as a layer-specific propagation artefact; the pre-registered gate requires only ≥1\geq 1 mid/late layer with positive CI excluding zero, satisfied by L57. A second readout records the agent’s realised next tool call under the forward-propagating patch: 0% shift toward AA at both L0 and L57, Δ\DeltaNLL→A≈0{}_{\to A}\approx 0. The forward-hook evidence is therefore representational propagation, not behavioural control.

Cross-family causal replication on Llama-3.3-70B. The same 80-minimal-pair protocol replicates on Llama-3.3-70B (80 decoder layers, hidden 8192). Patch layers {0,20,60,78}\{0,20,60,78\} chosen proportional to Qwen3’s {0,14,41,57}\{0,14,41,57\}.

Feature-level cross-family STRONG: Δpatch>0\Delta_{\mathrm{patch}}>0 with CI excluding zero at L60 (100% of 80 pairs) and L78 (98.75%); L0 control exactly zero. Forward-hook cross-family PARTIAL: representational propagation confirmed at L60 and L78 (CIs exclude zero); the L20 significant negative deflection is analogous to Qwen3 L41’s. Behavioural readout matches Qwen3 (0%0\% shift at L78, Δ\DeltaNLL→A≈0{}_{\to A}\approx 0): behaviour does not move on Llama either. The L60/L78 forward-propagation effects are ∼10×\sim 10\times Qwen3’s L57 magnitude, suggesting a stronger propagation-robust signal in the larger model.

Cross-benchmark collection protocols. All runs reuse the §3 probe and group logo folds / bootstrap resamples by task identity; effective NN is the distinct-task count. TaskBench: 200 single-shot planning instances; labels are TaskBench’s provided per-instance dependency DAG, not our substring oracle (1,504 pairs, 556 direct++ / 802 transitive++). BFCL multi_turn_base: 197 distinct stateful multi-turn tasks; structurally direct-only (1 transitive-only edge in 4,525 pairs). ComplexFuncBench: teacher-forced replay of the dataset’s golden interactive trajectories (real args + golden observations), residual captured at each assistant decision boundary; 400 Cross-* multi-hop tasks, 6,780 pairs (2,747 direct++ / 1,679 transitive++). ToolHop: free-generation agent loop with local-Python execution of the dataset’s own functions, residual at generation step 0; 994 productive tasks, 9,676 pairs (2,938 direct++ / 826 transitive++).

Cross-benchmark results. Direct AUROC: TaskBench 0.894, ComplexFuncBench 0.849, ToolHop 0.854, BFCL 0.960. Transitive AUROC: TaskBench 0.888, ComplexFuncBench 0.943, ToolHop 0.966. Non-positional contribution Δ\Delta resid−-pos (transitive task): ToolHop +0.161+0.161 (paired 95% CI [+0.142,+0.182][+0.142,+0.182], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0, position-only 0.805), ComplexFuncBench +0.060+0.060 (CI [+0.049,+0.071][+0.049,+0.071], P⁡(Δ≤0)=0P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0, position-only 0.872), TaskBench −0.020-0.020 (CI [−0.047,+0.007][-0.047,+0.007], position-only 0.891 — single-shot, position-trivial).

Viability heuristic. A pre-registered guard flags a benchmark position-trivial when its positional baseline exceeds 0.85. ComplexFuncBench (0.872) trips this guard yet its residual still contributes a significant +0.060+0.060 (P⁡(Δ≤0)=0P(\Delta{\leq}0){=}0); we report this explicitly (§4.2.2) so the heuristic flag is not read as a negative result. The guard’s intended target is the TaskBench regime, where the residual adds nothing.

Underpowered corroborations. A τ\tau-bench airline expansion yields effective N=13N{=}13 distinct productive task structures, below the pre-stated ≥15\geq 15 viability threshold; we do not report it as a powered cross-domain row. A τ2\tau^{2}-bench telecom run (free-generation Qwen3-32B with native tool calling on the Sierra τ2\tau^{2}-bench telecom env, 60 productive distinct tasks, 282 pairs, 206 direct++, 9 transitive++) falls below the pre-registered ≥30\geq 30 transitive++ trend-inclusion threshold but yields a significant positive Δ\Delta resid−-pos +0.269+0.269 (paired-bootstrap CI [+0.099,+0.388][+0.099,+0.388], P=0.0085P{=}0.0085, position-only 0.6600.660), recorded as an independent interactive∧\wedgemulti-hop corroboration of Claim B rather than a trend point.
